abstract: Neonicotinoids are widely used pesticides linked to impaired reproduction and population decline in birds. However, the behavioral mechanisms connecting exposure to reduced reproduction remain unclear. Here, we examined the effects of imidacloprid, one of the most commonly used neonicotinoids, on singing in male zebra finches. Birds received sublethal doses of imidacloprid through drinking water over 30 days, followed by a 30-day washout. Using continuous acoustic monitoring and female-presentation assays, we quantified non-courtship and female-directed courtship song and assessed body mass, locomotion, non-vocal displays, and song structure. During the 30-day drinking-water exposure, imidacloprid reduced daily non-courtship singing, with effects persisting into washout. It also reduced courtship song, whereas body mass, locomotion, non-vocal displays, and song structure showed no detectable treatment-related changes. In a separate experiment, acute imidacloprid injection also reduced courtship song but was accompanied by some non-vocal behavioral impairment. These findings identify song output as a sensitive behavioral endpoint for neonicotinoid toxicity, suggesting that even low doses might impair songbird reproduction by suppressing singing before conventional signs of toxicity become apparent. This suppression of song production implies that widespread neonicotinoid use could silently contribute to population declines in wild birds by compromising their ability to attract mates, defend territories, form pair bonds, and successfully breed. Song output may therefore complement conventional measures when assessing the sublethal effects of neonicotinoids in songbirds.

summary: Sublethal imidacloprid in drinking water reduced song output in male zebra finches, including courtship song, before other toxicity signs appeared.
title: 'Silent Spring' revisited: sublethal neonicotinoid exposure suppresses birdsong
